paras: The vessel lay alongside berth 4, loading iron ore, when she took a list of seven degrees to starboard. Loading was stopped, and the list was corrected over the following four hours by transferring ballast from the starboard tanks to the port side. No cargo was lost and nobody was injured, but the port authority suspended the operation for forty-eight hours.

The stability calculation submitted before loading showed the ship upright at every stage. The investigators concluded that those figures must have been produced from a plan that was never followed: the loading sequence on the manifest called for the two holds nearest the bow to be filled first, and the crane operators had begun amidships. A difference of that size could not have appeared without a change of sequence.

Two other explanations were entertained and discounted. The ballast pumps may have been running against a closed valve, which would have produced a slow list rather than a sudden one. A free surface effect in a partly filled tank could have made the list worse, although it could not have started it. Neither theory accounts for seven degrees in under twenty minutes.

The report notes that the pilot had left the vessel before loading began and that no stage of the loading plan was verified against the manifest at any point. The recommendation is that the officer of the watch confirm each stage against the document before the next hold is opened, and that the keel-to-deck stress figures be recalculated whenever the sequence changes.

The text says she 'lay alongside berth 4, loading iron ore, when she took a list of seven degrees to starboard'.
The stability figures submitted before loading had been fabricated.
The text says the figures 'must have been produced from a plan that was never followed'. That is a different claim: the numbers were real, the plan was not followed.

The text says the list 'was corrected over the following four hours by transferring ballast from the starboard tanks to the port side'.
The investigation discounted free surface effect altogether.
The text says it 'could have made the list worse, although it could not have started it'. It was not ruled out as a factor, only as the cause.

items.situation: The report says the figures must have been produced from another plan. Did anybody see that happen?
tips: No. Must have is the writer's conclusion, not a witnessed fact.
An option saying the text states it is claiming more than the page does.

items.situation: Which is stronger: the pumps may have been running, or the pumps must have been running?
tips: Must have is near certainty. May have is one possibility among several.
The report used may have, which means it was not chosen.

items.situation: Say, in exam register, that the ship leaned over to her right-hand side.
tips: She took a list to starboard.

items.situation: The text says free surface could not have started the list. Is free surface ruled out completely?
tips: No. It could have made the list worse; it could not have started it.
An option saying it was discounted altogether is too strong.

tips: The vessel was moored at her berth.

listenings.text: I was on deck when I felt her go over. It was not gradual. One moment we were upright, and inside twenty minutes we had seven degrees to starboard and the gangway was scraping the quay. I stopped the loading straight away and started transferring ballast from the starboard tanks to the port side. That took four hours. Nobody was hurt and we did not lose a single tonne of ore. What I still cannot explain is the plan. The manifest said the two holds nearest the bow first, and I watched the cranes start amidships. Somebody must have changed the sequence, and whoever changed it never told the bridge. The pilot had gone ashore before we opened the first hold, so there was nobody outside the ship to see it either.

When I board a ship I am not there to take her over. The master keeps command. What I bring is the water: I know where the bank is, where the current sets, and how the channel behaves on a falling tide. The first thing I ask for is the passage plan. I want to see every waypoint from the pilot station to the berth, with a time against it, and I want to know the draft the ship is leaving with, because that number decides everything else. If a waypoint on the plan does not match what I would do, we discuss it on the bridge before we move, not halfway down the channel. And if the plan has no waypoint for the turn into the basin, we make one. A plan that stops at the harbour entrance is not a plan.
